text: Flies: many types affect cattle — blood-sucking types cause blood loss (especially in young animals), skin lesions, and painful, constant annoyance; non-blood-sucking types annoy in large numbers (over 100 per animal), can spread bacteria/virus, and irritate the eyes' mucous membranes; flies laying eggs in wounds produce maggots that initially clean dead/infected tissue but, if uncontrolled, go on to eat healthy tissue too. Control products: Permethrin (Butox) or Coumaphos (Asuntol). Mosquitoes: feed mostly in late afternoon/night, breeding in water and favoring shaded resting areas — night-time biting disturbs sleep, leaving cattle too tired to graze well by day and causing loss of condition; control by burning leaves/weeds for smoke, or installing a mosquito net over the stable area at night. Ticks: on a lightly infested animal, check the tail butt, belly, shoulder, dewlap, and ears first; heavy infestation can cover the whole body. They cause blood loss and weakness (especially in calves), significant skin damage from their long mouthparts, and spread Babesia and Anaplasma. Control: Permethrin (Butox) or Coumaphos (Asuntol) for immediate effect, or Ivermectin (Ivomec), which reaches maximum effect 4–5 days after injection. Mites (mange): cause intense rubbing/scratching, hair loss, and thickened, crusty skin that can cover the whole body; hard to control since mites burrow into the hide — Ivermectin injection is the best option (Asuntol also works), with a second treatment 2–3 weeks later needed to match the parasite's life cycle.
